title: Dispersive Readout of a SiMOS Quantum Dot Using a Flip-Chip Integrated Microwave Resonator
authors: Vo Kim Hieu Van, Santiago Serrano, Cédric Bohémier, Ajit Dash, Fay E. Hudson, Tuomo Tanttu, Chih Hwan Yang, MengKe Feng, Ensar Vahapoglu, Florian K. Unseld, Wee Han Lim, Andrea Morello, Andrew S. Dzurak, Kok Wai Chan
abstract: Heterogeneous integration provides a promising route to combine semiconductor quantum dot devices and superconducting microwave circuits, while allowing each component to be fabricated using an optimized process flow. Here, we demonstrate a flip-chip integrated platform for dispersive readout of silicon metal-oxide semiconductor (SiMOS) quantum dot devices. A SiMOS double quantum dot chip is bonded to a superconducting aluminum resonator chip using indium bump interconnects to enable microwave coupling to the quantum dot gate. We show that the developed flip-chip process is compatible with cryogenic operation of both the SiMOS device and the superconducting resonator, and demonstrate resonator-based detection of charge transitions in the quantum dot system. The readout signal-to-noise ratio follows a dependence of $\sqrt{t}$ with the integration time, reaching SNR = 1 at an integration time of approximately 0.3 ms. These results establish flip-chip bonding as a viable integration approach for SiMOS quantum dot devices operating at both dc and microwave frequencies, with potential applications for resonator-based techniques such as spin-photon coupling.
summary: The research demonstrates the successful integration of SiMOS quantum dot devices with superconducting microwave resonators using a flip-chip bonding technique. By measuring changes in the resonator's response, they achieve dispersive readout of charge transitions in the quantum dots. This establishes a robust and scalable platform crucial for advancing solid-state quantum computing architectures.
main_problem: The primary goal is to demonstrate a viable, scalable integration method for reading out charge states in Silicon Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (SiMOS) quantum dot devices using superconducting microwave resonators.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated dispersive readout of SiMOS double quantum dots on a flip-chip integrated platform, showing that the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) scales as $\sqrt{t}$ and remains measurable across varying temperature and magnetic field regimes.
method: The experiment uses reflectometry measurements at cryogenic temperatures to couple microwave signals through an indium bump interconnect between the SiMOS QD chip and a superconducting aluminum resonator chip.
model_or_system: The system comprises a SiMOS double quantum dot (DQD) coupled capacitively to a superconducting aluminum resonator. The readout mechanism relies on measuring shifts in the resonator's frequency or transmission spectrum due to changes in the DQD's charge state.
key_observables: Resonator resonance frequency ($f_r$), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), DC transport current ($I_{dc}$), and electrochemical-potential noise spectrum ($	ext{S}_{\mu}(f)$).
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures (down to 60 mK), integration time dependence ($\propto \sqrt{t}$), magnetic field range (up to 10 mT), and coupling regimes (strongly/weakly coupled).
main_assumptions: The superconducting resonator properties are sensitive to temperature and magnetic fields, which limits the readout performance; the $	ext{SNR} \propto \sqrt{t}$ dependence suggests white noise limited measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device architecture (SEM images), charge stability maps showing transitions in different coupling regimes, and quantitative plots demonstrating SNR scaling with integration time and input power, alongside temperature/field dependencies for both microwave response and DC current.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical setup using flip-chip bonding to integrate SiMOS QDs and superconducting resonators. It then presents characterization results by measuring charge stability maps, quantifying readout performance via SNR analysis across varying environmental parameters (T, B), and finally analyzing noise spectra.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses scalability in solid-state quantum computing by proving a robust, integrated platform for coupling qubits (the QD) to high-quality microwave measurement circuits (the resonator).
